notes.meaning: Paul traveled along the inland roads of the region and arrived in the major port city of Ephesus, keeping a earlier promise to return. Apollos had already departed to minister in Corinth across the sea. In Ephesus, Paul came across a small group of religious followers who were known as disciples.

Paul noticed that something was missing in the spiritual life of these disciples and asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit. They answered that they had never even heard that the Holy Spirit had been given. They likely knew about the Spirit from the Old Testament, but they did not know that God's promised Spirit had already been poured out at Pentecost.

differ.view: Every true believer receives the Holy Spirit at conversion, so these events reflect the unique historical spread of the gospel rather than a regular two-step experience.
These men were not yet born-again Christians because anyone who belongs to Christ already has the Holy Spirit dwelling inside them.

notes.meaning: Paul asked what baptism they had received, since Christian baptism includes the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The men replied that they had only received John the Baptist's baptism. This showed Paul that their instruction stopped before the full Christian message had reached them.

Paul explained that John's baptism was meant to prepare people by calling them to turn away from sin and point them forward. John told everyone to put their trust in the greater One coming after him. That promised Savior was Jesus, whose arrival fulfilled everything John announced.

Once the men understood the full truth about Jesus, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. This brought them into the full fellowship and life of the Christian church. This is the only place in the New Testament where people who had received John's baptism were baptized again.

Paul placed his hands on them in prayer, and the Holy Spirit came upon them with power. They began speaking in languages they had never learned and proclaiming God's message with inspired speech. This visible sign confirmed that these believers were now fully included in the body of Christ, just like the believers at Pentecost.
The entire group consisted of about twelve men. They became the first core group of believers in the growing church at Ephesus.

Paul went into the local Jewish synagogue and preached with boldness every Sabbath for three months. He reasoned with the people and tried to persuade them that Jesus had inaugurated God's promised rule. The listeners in Ephesus tolerated his message far longer than synagogues in other cities had.

Eventually, some of the listeners became stubborn, refused to believe, and openly insulted the Christian way of life in front of the crowd. Paul decided to withdraw the believers from the synagogue so they would not be pulled away. He rented or borrowed the lecture hall of a teacher named Tyrannus and taught there every day.

Paul kept up this daily teaching routine for two full years in the hall. Because Ephesus was a major trade center, travelers carried the message to the surrounding towns. As a result, both Jews and Greeks throughout the entire Roman province of Asia heard the gospel.

God performed unusual and astonishing miracles through Paul while he ministered in Ephesus. People carried away work aprons and face cloths that Paul had used, and when these touched the sick, illnesses were healed and evil spirits were driven out. The power came entirely from God, who met people in their simple faith to show that Christ was greater than any local magic.

Some wandering Jewish exorcists made their living by going from town to town trying to cast out demons with spoken charms. Seeing Paul's success, they tried using the name of Jesus like a magic spell. They commanded the evil spirits to leave by the authority of Jesus whom Paul preached.

Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva were among those attempting this practice. Sceva likely claimed a high priestly title to give himself and his sons more prestige in their magical trade.

The evil spirit inside the possessed man spoke back and refused to obey them. The demon acknowledged that it recognized Jesus' authority and was well aware of Paul, but demanded to know who these men thought they were. The spirit knew they were impostors who had no real faith or authority in Christ.

The man controlled by the demon sprang violently on the brothers with terrifying strength. He battered them, tore off their clothes, and overpowered them so completely that all seven fled out of the house naked and bleeding. This shocking defeat proved that Satan's power cannot be broken by mere formulas without true faith.

Word of what happened to Sceva's sons quickly spread among all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. A deep and holy reverence fell over the whole city. People realized that Jesus was not a charm to be trifled with, and his name was held in the highest honor.

Many people who had already accepted faith in Christ came forward to openly confess wrong things they had kept hidden. Seeing the reality and danger of demonic power drove them to clean out all secret ties to the occult. True repentance led them to bring their private sins into the light.

A large number of people who practiced sorcery gathered up their costly spell books and burned them in public. When the value of the destroyed scrolls was added up, it came to fifty thousand silver coins, equal to thousands of days of wages. Burning the books proved they were truly done with their old way of life and refused to let anyone else be harmed by them.

Through these striking events, the message of the Lord grew steadily in influence and won great victories over darkness. The gospel proved itself far stronger than the deep-rooted superstitions and magic of the city.
